title: The intention to fast
hook: the intention for Ramadan, made each night or once for the month, by school

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last day on zakat, and your line: given through many hands. Collectors, mosques, funds, charities. Did you thank someone who carries help to others? Today, a new pillar: the fast. Day one thousand one hundred five.

Skip breakfast and lunch, and by afternoon the body can't tell why. Too busy to eat? Or fasting? Same empty stomach, same slump, same glance at the clock. The difference is invisible, and it happened before the day even started: someone decided. The Islamic fast begins not at dawn with the first hunger but earlier, in the mind, with a word the legal books set at the start of acts of worship. Today, the intention to fast.
screen: `AN EMPTY STOMACH BY AFTERNOON.` → `FORGOT, OR FASTED?` → `THE DIFFERENCE CAME FIRST.`

segments.voice: First, the command itself. Surah two, in Pickthall's translation: "O ye who believe! Fasting is prescribed for you, even as it was prescribed for those before you, that ye may ward off (evil)." The fast has a purpose, and a purpose needs someone who means it. Second, the word is niyyah, intention. The collection of Imam al-Bukhari opens with a saying of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: actions are judged by intentions, and each person gets what they intended. That's why a forgotten lunch and a fast aren't the same. Another report, in the Sunan of Abu Dawud and others, ties this directly to fasting: whoever doesn't resolve to fast before dawn has no fast. Third, scholars ask a practical question: how often? Here the schools differ. Some, such as the Shafi'i and Hanbali schools, teach that the intention for each obligatory day of Ramadan is made each night, before dawn. The Maliki school holds that a single intention at the start of the month can cover the whole of it, as long as the fast isn't broken off. The Hanafi school allows the intention for a Ramadan day to be made later, before about the middle of the day, if nothing has been eaten. Shia jurists have their own rulings too. Each school has its reasons, and Muslims follow the school they belong to. Fourth, where intention lives. The jurists place it in the heart, not on the tongue; some count waking for the pre-dawn meal as a sign of it. Some say a spoken intention helps focus the mind, others think saying it aloud isn't needed. Outside Ramadan, the lesson travels: the same act can be two different things, depending on what you meant by it.
screen: `FASTING IS PRESCRIBED FOR YOU.` · `NIYYAH: ACTIONS BY INTENTIONS.` · `EACH NIGHT, OR ONCE: BY SCHOOL.` · `IN THE HEART, NOT THE TONGUE.` · then, large: `THAT YE MAY WARD OFF (EVIL).`

segments.voice: The practice: set an intention tonight, and begin now. Settle, and breathe. Pick one thing you'll do tomorrow that you'd normally do without thinking: a meal, a commute, a meeting, a call to your mother. Decide now what you mean by it. Not what you'll get out of it. What it's for. Hold that one sentence in your mind for these two minutes. If you're planning a fast, you can make its intention tonight, in the way your school teaches. Tonight, before you sleep, come back to it once. The bell holds the time.
The intention to fast. Niyyah: resolving in the heart, before dawn, to fast for Allah; each night or once for the month, depending on the school. Today's word.
Your line: intend it. Today, before one ordinary thing, stop for a second and decide what it's for. Day one thousand one hundred five.

howItsDone: Muslims make the intention to fast in the heart before dawn; Shafi'i and Hanbali Muslims renew it each night of Ramadan, Malikis may make one intention for the month, and Hanafis may make it until around midday for a Ramadan fast.

trapdoor: what you thought: fasting is not eating.
what it means: fasting is not eating with intention, resolved before dawn.
what a scholar hears: niyyah for each day or once for the month is a classic point where the schools differ; Bukhari's collection opens with the intentions report.

notes: Pickthall 2:183 quoted from memory; confirm exact wording.
Abu Dawud 2454 (no fast for whoever does not resolve it before dawn): confirm number and grading; also in Tirmidhi and Nasa'i.

School positions: Shafi'i/Hanbali nightly; Maliki one intention for the month if not interrupted; Hanafi allows the Ramadan intention until before the 'midday' (dahwa kubra) if nothing eaten. Confirm all; Shia (Ja'fari) rulings are mentioned without detail.
'The legal books place it in the heart': confirm. The note that some recommend verbalizing (talaffuz) and others do not: confirm fair.
Practice invites only those 'planning a fast' to make a fasting intention; no new prayer or formula is given.
